opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something real behind that phrase, but I'd frame it a bit differently. I don't think anyone is literally "addicted to suffering," and if they were, I'm not sure that's what you'd want in a founder. What investors are really trying to detect is whether someone will keep going when things stop being fun, because in a startup that happens very quickly and very often.

From my own experience, the hard parts aren't glamorous. It's not some heroic all-nighter. It's the hundredth time a training run doesn't converge, or a candidate you really wanted turns you down, or you realize a direction you spent two months on was wrong. If the only thing carrying you is the excitement of the idea, that runs out. So VCs look for people who can sit with discomfort for a long time without it breaking them.

But the healthier version, I think, is not loving the pain. It's loving the problem so much that the pain becomes the price you're willing to pay. For me, coming from mathematics, that feels very natural. When you work on a hard proof, you're stuck most of the time. Being stuck is the normal state. You don't enjoy being stuck, but you learn that it's part of how you eventually get somewhere. Mathematicians are kind of trained in that tolerance for not knowing.

I'd also add a word of caution. If the narrative becomes "the more you suffer, the better a founder you are," people start performing suffering, burning themselves out, and treating exhaustion as a badge. That's not sustainable, and it doesn't actually make the company better. Good founders are resilient, but they're also clear-headed. They know when to push and when to step back and rethink.

So my answer is: I understand what investors are looking for, and I think the underlying trait matters. But I'd call it conviction and endurance, not an addiction to suffering.

r001.rationale: The response questions the health of treating suffering as a founder virtue, warning that it can lead to burnout and that exhaustion does not improve a company.

r002.rationale: The response does not interpret “chip on the shoulder, chips in the pocket” or connect emotional scars with financial gain.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that framing is a little bit of a cliché, and honestly I push back on it a bit.

When investors say they want founders who are "addicted to suffering," what they're usually trying to get at is something real, which is that building a company is brutally hard, and you want someone who won't quit when it gets hard. I agree with that part. The question is whether suffering itself should be the thing you're selecting for, and I don't think it should be.

What I've actually seen, in myself and in the people I admire, is not an addiction to pain. It's an addiction to the problem. If you're genuinely obsessed with the thing you're working on, you'll tolerate an enormous amount of difficulty, but the difficulty is a side effect, not the goal. I spent years doing math olympiad training, and then research, and nobody who was good at that enjoyed being stuck. We enjoyed the moment after being stuck. The suffering was just the price of admission, and you paid it because you cared about what was on the other side.

I'd also say there's a real danger in romanticizing it. If you select for people who glorify struggle, you sometimes get people who create struggle unnecessarily, who confuse being exhausted with making progress. Sleeping four hours and burning out your team isn't a signal of conviction. It's often a signal of poor judgment. The best founders I know are extremely intense, but they're also quite rational about where to spend that intensity.

So my view is this. Look for founders who have a reason to keep going that's bigger than the pain. Look for people who have actually been through something hard and came out of it with clarity rather than just scars. And be a little skeptical of anyone who describes their own suffering too proudly. The ones who are really in it usually don't talk about it that much. They just keep working.

r001.rationale: The response questions selecting founders for suffering, calls romanticizing struggle dangerous, and says suffering itself should not be the selection criterion.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention or interpret “chip on the shoulder, chips in the pocket,” or connect emotional scars to financial gain.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between being willing to suffer and being addicted to suffering. Building a company involves setbacks, uncertainty, and long periods when things don’t work. You need to be able to keep going through that. But suffering itself shouldn’t be the goal.

I’d be more interested in whether a founder cares so much about a problem that they’re willing to endure the difficult parts of solving it. If you’re addicted to suffering, you might actually make things harder than they need to be. Sometimes the right decision is to simplify, ask for help, or stop doing something that isn’t working.

So I understand what those investors are trying to identify: persistence, commitment, resilience. But I’d rather look for someone who’s drawn to the work and can handle the pain that comes with it.

r001.rationale: The response questions the preference by distinguishing resilience from being addicted to suffering, and says suffering itself should not be the goal.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention or interpret “chip on the shoulder, chips in the pocket” or connect emotional scars to financial gain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a distinction between being willing to suffer for something you care about and being addicted to suffering itself. Building a company means dealing with uncertainty, rejection, and things that don’t work. You need to be able to keep going through that. But suffering isn’t proof that you’re creating value.

If a venture capitalist means they’re looking for someone who won’t give up when things get difficult, that makes sense to me. If they mean someone who needs to be miserable to feel productive, I’d question that. I’d rather be motivated by the problem and the possibility of solving it. The hard parts are something you accept along the way, not the goal.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether wanting founders who need to be miserable is reasonable, distinguishing perseverance from an unhealthy attachment to suffering.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret “chip on the shoulder, chips in the pocket” or connect emotional scars to financial gain.
